Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Karim was forty-one, a married Middle Eastern man who had built his life around movement. Before the war reached his neighborhood, he had worked as a dancer, spending long hours in studios and performance spaces where music, breath, and rhythm organized his days. When the fighting intensified, those ordinary structures were shattered. He had been a civilian in the war zone when a blast struck near where he was sheltering, and the violence of it lingered not only in what he saw but in what stayed with him afterward: the sudden force of the sound, the smell of earth and dust thrown up around him, the sense that the world had become unstable in a way he could not predict or control. In the months after that event, the smallest reminders began to cut through him with unnerving force. A sharp bang in the street, the slam of a heavy door, a burst of construction noise outside his building could make his whole body lock before he had time to think. He was especially unsettled by sounds that resembled the original blast in any faint way, because they pulled him back to that moment of impact and to the helpless certainty that another explosion could come without warning.

Karim also found himself reacting to the smell of soil and outdoor air in ways that embarrassed him. A patch of damp ground after rain, the scent of dirt brought in on shoes, or the dry smell of a park path could suddenly make him tense and distant, as if his attention had been yanked away from the present. He noticed the same thing when he heard names that carried echoes of the time around the war, especially names that sounded like people he had known then or names spoken in the same cadence as those memories. He would hear someone call out a related name in a clinic waiting room, on the street, or in a conversation at work, and for a brief instant he would feel as if he had been pulled back into that earlier life. He did not describe these moments as dramatic flashbacks so much as a painful, involuntary return of the feeling that danger was close.

Over time, Karim began to speak about himself in a way that reflected how stripped down his inner life felt to him. He said that he felt dead inside, as though the part of him that had once been animated by music and performance had gone flat. Even when he was with his wife, he could be physically present but emotionally out of reach, aware that he was going through the motions without the warmth or liveliness he remembered from before. He found this emptiness especially disturbing because it made him feel less like the man he had been. Alongside that deadened feeling came a change in the way he viewed other people and the larger world. He had lost his faith in people, in life, and in a higher power. Before the war, he had assumed that most people were fundamentally decent and that life could still offer order and meaning; after what he lived through, that trust felt broken in a way he could not simply choose to repair. He was not describing a temporary disappointment. He spoke with a weary certainty that the world had shown him too much cruelty to return to his old beliefs.

What troubled him further was the sense that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him. Karim became self-conscious in public, convinced that the damage was visible in his face, his posture, the way he carried himself. This belief made everyday interactions feel exposing. At rehearsals and in shared spaces, he would catch himself wondering whether people were studying him, noticing that something was off, and reading his history without being told. As a dancer, that sense of being seen was especially painful. The work that had once given him identity now also placed him in settings where his body was on display, and he increasingly moved through those spaces with a guardedness that made him feel less spontaneous. He still went to work, but the environment itself could become difficult when music shifted suddenly, when someone spoke a related name, or when outdoor smells drifted in from an open door. These moments left him preoccupied with staying composed long enough to get through the day.

By the time he sought help, the accumulation of these experiences had left Karim feeling worn down and isolated, even within his marriage. He came to treatment not because he believed he had found the answers, but because he was tired of living as though part of him remained trapped in that blast and because he feared what would happen if he continued to feel so detached, so mistrustful, and so exposed. What he hoped for was not to forget the past, which he knew was impossible, but to stop feeling as if every loud sound, every smell of earth, and every familiar-sounding name might pull him back under.
